rich_summary: After celestial nymphs fail to disturb the ascetic three‑headed son of Twashtri, Indra decides to eliminate the potential threat. He strikes the ascetic with his thunderbolt and, still fearful of the corpse’s lingering power, orders a carpenter to sever the heads. From the three mouths burst different birds, symbolizing the being’s varied practices. Twashtri, enraged at the unjust killing of his innocent son, creates the mighty demon Vritra to destroy Indra. Vritra nearly defeats the gods, even swallowing Indra, until the gods seek Vishnu’s aid. Through diplomacy and deception, Indra exploits a loophole in Vritra’s protective boon and kills him with sea‑foam infused with Vishnu’s power. Yet victory brings no peace: Indra is overwhelmed by guilt and the sin of Brahmanicide, hides himself, and the cosmos falls into disorder without a king of the gods.

highlight_spans.why: Shows the failure of the celestial nymphs and Indra’s shift from temptation to violent strategy against the ascetic.
Indra’s thunderbolt kills the three‑headed being, a pivotal act that triggers the chain of vengeance leading to Vritra’s creation.
Twashtri’s furious vow and the creation of Vritra mark the emotional and mythic turning point of the narrative.
Indra exploits the loophole in Vritra’s boon, killing him with sea foam and Vishnu’s hidden power—an iconic example of divine cunning.
After victory, Indra is crushed by guilt and the sin of Brahmanicide, leading to cosmic disorder when the king of the gods disappears.

top_scenes.scene_text: Indra hurls his blazing thunderbolt at the towering three‑headed ascetic, whose massive body crashes to the earth like a fallen mountain.
When the severed heads fall, flocks of birds—partridges, quails, and sparrows—burst dramatically from the three mouths into the sky.
At twilight on the seashore, Indra throws a hill‑sized mass of sea‑foam infused with Vishnu’s hidden power toward the colossal Vritra.
